title: FIFA insists ‘nobody is selling football’, pushes ahead with consultation plan despite backlash
content:
FIFA has insisted “nobody is selling football” after criticism of its decision to launch a consultation on selling stakes in a World Cup commercial entity to private investors.

The world governing body of football stopped short of saying it would be withdrawing the plan and instead reaffirmed its commitment to press ahead with the consultation period.

It comes as the Asian Football Confederation (AFC), joined the European confederation UEFA and Concacaf, the confederation of North, Central America and the Caribbean, in rejecting FIFA’s notion of selling stakes in the World Cup.

The Athletic reported FIFA president Gianni Infantino’s future leadership of the organisation was questioned during the meetings of UEFA and Concacaf on Thursday.

UEFA and Concacaf released statements rejecting the plans following their respective meetings, with UEFA announcing that all 55 European members would boycott all FIFA competitions unless the proposals were abandoned.

The AFC, Concacaf and UEFA make up 137 of the 211 FIFA member associations.

On Friday, FIFA responded to say it “acknowledges and respects feedback and concern aired in public” but was pressing on with its proposals, adding that the body “reaffirms its commitment to an open and democratic consultation”.

It said FIFA Forward Enterprises (FFE), the new entity which would take over FIFA’s commercial operations, “has been proposed solely to ensure that all FIFA member associations (MAs) have the opportunity to take meaningful ownership of the commercial opportunity of football in their respective countries, and that this does not come at the cost of either the spirit or the governance of FIFA or football itself.”

It added: “Nobody is selling football. This is not something FIFA would ever entertain.

“Everyone has the right to express their opposition and to seek further clarification but no single entity can claim to represent all 211 MAs around the world.”

FIFA has also confirmed that if MAs are opposed to the FFE plan but the proposal passes, those opposed will still receive $20million (£14.9m) each in the 2027-30 cycle (followed by $22m in 2031-34 and $24m in 2035-38), irrespective of whether any stake in FFE is sold to private investors.

However, if that MA agrees to the FFE proposal, it will receive $40million in 2027-30, with the subsequent payments to remain the same.

Notably, FIFA’s statement indicated, and The Athletic has since confirmed, that the proposal directly ties the creation of FFE to an accompanying sell-off to external investors.

There is nothing stopping FIFA from creating FFE as a new, focused commercial entity and retaining 100 per cent of it; one source told The Athletic that was “eminently feasible”. Revenues would, at least theoretically, improve by the hiving out of commercial and events operations, and member payments would improve as a result, regardless of whether any sell-off took place.

But that is not FIFA’s proposal. It is not either-or. Members will have to vote for the creation of FFE and its partial sell-off, or decline to see FFE introduced at all. It is a crucial distinction.

Asian football’s governing body, the AFC, said on Friday it “stands in solidarity” with counterparts UEFA and Concacaf over objections to FIFA’s plans.

The AFC expressed “serious concerns” over the process and said of suggestions of a boycott of the World Cup: “Football should never have been placed in such a position.”

It was a damning statement, attacking the “unprecedented divisions” which had been created in the sport’s governing bodies and cast doubt on the potential for FFE to pass through FIFA’s membership. “Any proposal that risks undermining the unity and universal character of the competition must be reconsidered,” the AFC added.

The AFC then went further, express concerns beyond FEE. “The AFC considers this issue extends far beyond a single proposal,” it continued. “Rather, it has exposed fundamental weaknesses in FIFA’s consultation and decision-making processes that must now be addressed. While the AFC notes FIFA’s latest clarification on the proposal, the central concerns surrounding governance, institutional process and meaningful consultation remain unanswered.”

It continued: “The primary objective for world football must be to ensure that decisions of such magnitude are being developed through processes that are anchored on transparency and command the confidence of the football community.

“This is not the first occasion where major stakeholders have been confronted with significant initiatives after the direction of travel appears to have already been determined. Such an approach undermines confidence in FIFA’s governance framework and diminishes the authority of its statutory bodies. No subsequent consultation process, however well intentioned, can replace early engagement with the appropriate FIFA bodies and the football family.

“The AFC believes this moment must become a catalyst for strengthening institutional reform. While every FIFA MA must have the opportunity to consider and determine proposals affecting the future of world football, meaningful democracy is not measured solely by the opportunity to vote. It begins with transparent governance, timely consultation, informed deliberation and genuine participation throughout the decision-making process.”

Analysis by The Athletic’s football finance expert Chris Weatherspoon

FIFA’s tying of FFE’s very creation to the immediate partial sell-off to private investors is a key distinction that has broadly been missed to date.

FIFA has several subsidiaries already, and there’s nothing stopping them shifting commercial operations into FFE without a member vote. The proposal put forward states that, even without the $4.2billion expected from an equity sale, running events under a standalone, focused entity like FFE would generate big sums for members: $4.2bn (separate to the equity proceeds) in 2027-30, $4.6bn in 2031-34 and $5.1bn in 2035-38.

Whether those sums are realistic without the arrival of external expertise is uncertain. One source familiar with FIFA’s thinking has told The Athletic that some of those increased revenues would be derived from bringing onboard new parties and commercially-focused staff.

Without them, FFE would just be comprised of existing staff in a new entity; there’d be a limit to how far revenues could improve. Still, that focus should engender some improvements, and there’s also nothing stopping FIFA just hiring better staff if they really think the current lot aren’t maximising turnover.

But it is now clear the latter isn’t an option anyway. FIFA’s proposal to members is absolute: FFE with an accompanying stake sale, or no FFE at all.

That is important to the calculus here as FIFA are, in effect, saying they won’t make a move toward revenue maximisation without getting approval to sell a stake, and it is the latter which has caused global consternation. Members who say no to the sale would also be, in effect, saying no to an internal shift toward better commercial performance.

FIFA could set FFE up, improve processes and retain ownership without external stakeholders. That would be similar to what has happened elsewhere, like at UC3 under UEFA, who have come out so strongly against this.

Instead, FFE, and thus the full multi-million dollar uplift — not just that one-off $20m from the equity sale — now being offered to members over the next 12 years lives or dies on whether those same members agree to sell a slice of the game.

On Tuesday, it was revealed that FIFA wanted to set up a new private entity — FIFA Forward Enterprise — to manage the commercial operations of its showpiece events, including the World Cup. As part of the plans, FIFA announced it was looking to sell a 21 per cent minority stake in FFE to outside investors. FIFA said the company was valued at $20billion (£14.8bn) by global bank JPMorgan Chase.

Thrive Capital, a company founded by Joshua Kushner, brother of U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, is expected to head up the proposed investor group.

To entice its 211 member associations, FIFA president Gianni Infantino said they would be in line to receive $40million in FIFA’s next four-year cycle if they backed this plan. He then gave them just 53 days to support the proposals — or miss out on the potential windfall.

For the scheme to go through, however, FIFA needs a majority of its 211 member associations and approval from the 37 members of the FIFA Council.

Coming just weeks after the conclusion of a World Cup dogged by controversy — including extortionate ticket prices, commercial breaks in each half dressed up as hydration breaks, President Trump intervening to overturn a red card shown to United States striker Folarin Balogun, and a surreal first ever half-time show in the final — and following Infantino’s extraordinary Instagram meltdown, the proposals have only intensified criticism of FIFA and its boss.

Tom Burrows

As soon as the plans became public, UEFA issued a swift and scathing response, saying they “cross a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross”.

It went on to say how “the soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA’s to sell”.

UEFA and its 55 member associations later gathered for a virtual meeting on Thursday, with more than 40 of them speaking out against the proposals. The body later put out an uncompromising new statement, saying no UEFA national teams would take part in any FIFA competition until the proposals were shelved.

“Some things are simply too important to sell,” it added. “The FIFA World Cup belongs to football. It always will. And so long as Europe has a voice, it will never be for sale.”

UEFA taking such a strong stance puts Infantino in a very sticky spot.

Tom Burrows
